## My Reasoning

I've been working this land in Quzhou for over 40 years. The North China Plain gives me one clear answer: winter wheat followed by summer maize on the same fields. That double-cropping rotation is what this county does, what the soil and the rainfall pattern support, and what the grain markets here are built around. I'm not going to change that at 65.

I farm about 10 mu — my own 8 mu plus 2 mu I lease from a neighbor who moved to Shijiazhuang years ago. At my age I hire contractors for the big mechanized jobs: seeding, harvesting. My son helps when he can.

For wheat I'll use Kenong 199 again. It's an improved variety, well-adapted here, good resistance to stripe rust, and I know what it does in my fields. I'll do rotary tillage in October before sowing. I'll skip the fourth irrigation this year — the groundwater table under Quzhou has been dropping my whole adult life. Three irrigations, timed well at jointing, heading, and grain filling, is enough if the winter isn't too dry. I've talked with the people from China Agricultural University's station here. They've convinced me on water reduction.

For the maize I switch to hybrid — Xianyu 335. No-till, direct-seeded immediately after wheat harvest in June. Summer rainfall usually covers most of the water needs. One supplemental irrigation at tasseling if July stays dry. Minimal pesticide — one application watching for fall armyworm.

I apply fertilizer based on the soil test results I got two seasons ago. I've cut my nitrogen back from what my neighbors still use. High input doesn't mean high return once you're past the optimum.
